newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: Landsbergis unseats old Communist foes in Lithuania vote.
newsitem.headline: Landsbergis unseats old Communist foes in Lithuania vote.

text.p: Lithuanian independence leader Vytautas Landsbergis claimed victory over his former Communist foes on Monday as parliamentary elections in the Baltic state put him back into office.
Avenging a shock defeat at the polls in 1992, Landsbergis' Homeland Union party had won 29 percent of the vote in the first round with 1,495 of the 2,037 voting districts counted.
The Christian Democrats were second with 10 percent and the former governing Lithuanian Democratic Labour Party (LDLP) third with just less than 10 percent.
The LDLP conceded defeat and Landsbergis named Gediminas Vagnorius as candidate for prime minister, a post he occupied under Landsbergis in 1991.

The first round of the vote decides 70 of the 141 seats in parliament under a proportional representation party list vote. The remaining 71 seats are decided on a majority vote and a second round run off will be held on November 10.
The Homeland Union was widely expected to form a rightwing coalition with the Christian Democrats and possibly also the Centre Union, which stood in fourth place on eight percent.

"We can say that our party won a victory in the first round and we do not think that after all the votes are counted there will be any significant changes that could affect our leading position," Landsbergis said.
The short and stocky Landsbergis, a former music professor, was the unlikely leader of the Baltic state's dramatic independence bid from the former Soviet Union.

He won much admiration for himself and his people by standing up to Moscow's might, especially after 13 people were killed by Soviet troops on an attack on Vilnius television tower, protected by civilians behind makeshift barricades.
But his popularity plumetted as his Sajudis independence movement was riven by faction-fighting and the economy collapsed after independence.
He suffered a humiliating defeat at the polls in 1992 when Lithuanians overwhelmingly backed the LDLP.
The LDLP said on Monday it was ready to work as the opposition. "The people put more hope in us than we could objectively fulfill," said LDLP speaker of parliament Cheslovas Jurshenas.
A low turnout of just 55 percent took some of the shine from Landsbergis' win, compared with the exceptionally high 1992 level of 75 percent.

As Landsbergis prepared for talks on a coalition, President Algirdas Brazauskas appealed for stability. Brazauskas, former LDLP leader, sealed the party's return to power by becoming president in 1993.
"Continuity is an imperative and the new government should continue the work of the previous government," Brazauskas said on Lithuanian radio.
Brazauskas, now without party affiliation, is set for a period of cooperation with a rightwing bloc.
Landsbergis, who when in opposition constantly sniped at the LDLP for corruption, said he wanted to start work with a "clean pair of hands".
"We want to see a Lithuania as different as possible from the Lithuania under Communists," he told reporters.
"The Lithuania under ex-communists was no different from the Lithuania under communists," he added.

The LDLP were propelled back into power on a platform of promises to ease the pain of the country's reform to a market economy. But instead of carrying out its populist pledges, it followed International Monetary Fund-inspired austerity policies.
The party was badly hurt at the end of last year when a former prime minister withdrew his personal savings from a bank days before it was closed at the start of a banking crisis.
